title: How satellites stay in orbit
examples: If gravity pulls everything down, how do satellites not just fall to Earth?
What is the difference between a regular orbit and a geostationary orbit?
Does a satellite need to be moving really fast to stay up there?

explain.say: We say that gravity is a force that pulls objects toward each other.
Now let me show you the real thing in 3D: a satellite in orbit. Look at the earth, the satellite and the solar panels. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.
A satellite is constantly falling toward Earth, but it keeps missing.
To stay in orbit, the satellite must have a very high orbital speed.

draw.text: High speed keeps satellite in orbit.

explain.say: Geostationary orbits mean the satellite stays over one spot always.
Think about a ball tied to a string being spun around your head.
A real life example is how GPS satellites keep their path steady.

faq.q: If gravity pulls everything down, why don't satellites just fall to Earth?
faq.a: The satellite is moving sideways so fast that as it falls, the Earth's surface curves away beneath it. It is constantly falling but always missing.
asks: How do they not crash into Earth?
What keeps them from falling down?

faq.q: What does 'orbital speed' actually mean for a satellite?
faq.a: It means the specific horizontal speed the satellite must maintain to balance the pull of gravity. If it slows down, it falls; if it speeds up, it might escape.
asks: Is speed the most important thing?
How fast does it need to go?

faq.q: What is the difference between a normal orbit and a geostationary orbit?
faq.a: A normal orbit moves across the sky over time, while a geostationary orbit appears to hang over the same spot on Earth constantly.
asks: Does GEO mean it stays put?

faq.q: Do all satellites need the same speed to orbit?
faq.a: No, the required speed changes depending on how high up the satellite is. Lower orbits require much higher speeds.
asks: Does height change the speed needed?

faq.q: Is gravity the only force involved in keeping a satellite up?
faq.a: Gravity is the main force pulling it, but the satellite's constant forward motion is what keeps it in its curved path.

facts: Gravity pulls all objects with mass toward each other.
Satellites need high horizontal speed to maintain orbit.
A geostationary orbit appears fixed over one point on Earth.
The speed needed changes with the altitude of the orbit.

quiz.say: If a satellite slows down while orbiting Earth, what will happen?
quiz.show: Slow speed causes satellite to fall.

options.show: It will fall closer to Earth.
options.say: It will fall closer to Earth.

quiz.why: Slowing down means gravity has a stronger pull relative to the speed, causing it to drop.

wrong.1: This is wrong because slowing down reduces the outward momentum needed to counteract gravity.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the primary effect of losing speed is falling downwards.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the satellite will enter a rapid, decaying fall, not just stop.

quiz.say: Which orbit keeps the satellite fixed over one spot?
quiz.why: Geostationary means it appears to stay in the same place relative to Earth's surface.

wrong.0: This is wrong because an escape orbit leaves Earth's gravitational pull entirely.
wrong.2: This is wrong because low orbits move very quickly across the sky.
wrong.3: This is wrong because polar orbits pass over the poles, changing location constantly.

quiz.say: If a satellite needs to move faster to stay up high, what happens to its path?

options.show: It will fall back to Earth.
options.say: It will fall back to Earth.

options.show: It will crash into the atmosphere.
options.say: It will crash into the atmosphere.

options.show: It will maintain a higher, stable orbit.
options.say: It will maintain a higher, stable orbit.

quiz.why: More speed means it covers more distance in the same time, keeping it further away from Earth.

wrong.0: This is wrong because increasing speed counteracts the pull of gravity more effectively.
wrong.1: This is wrong because the question asks what happens when it moves faster.
wrong.2: This is wrong because speed helps it avoid the drag and pull of the lower atmosphere.
